title: The Implicit Default
blurb: Leave the modifier off and C# picks one for you — and it's different depending on where you are. Sort each declaration by the accessibility it gets by default. The legend has the rules.

glossary.private: Default for MEMBERS of a class or struct (fields, methods, nested types). Forget a modifier inside a class and it's private.
glossary.internal: Default for TOP-LEVEL types declared in a namespace (class, struct, interface, enum, delegate) — visible assembly-wide, but not outside it.
glossary.public: Default for INTERFACE members and ENUM members: an interface exists to expose a contract, and enum values are always public (you can't even change it).

levels.title: L1 · Where does it default?
levels.prompt: No access modifier is written. What accessibility does each get?

items.label: a top-level class in a namespace

failStates.title: Top-level types default to internal
failStates.explain: A class declared in a namespace is internal unless you write public. Lots of people assume 'no modifier = public' — it's the opposite outside a type.

failStates.title: Interface members are public
failStates.explain: The whole point of an interface is to expose a contract, so its members are public by default (and pre-C# 8 couldn't be anything else).

items.label: a nested class inside a class
a top-level struct in a namespace
a delegate declared in a namespace
a property inside a record class

failStates.title: A nested type is a member
failStates.explain: Unlike a top-level type, a class nested inside another class is a member — so it defaults to private, just like a field.

failStates.title: Enum members are always public
failStates.explain: You can't apply any access modifier to enum members — they're public, full stop.

failStates.title: record doesn't change member defaults
failStates.explain: The record modifier synthesizes extra members but doesn't change accessibility — a member inside a record class still defaults to private.
